introduction: A hundred passages on the love of God, arranged in eight movements: love received and returned, knowing the Beloved, purifying the heart, the language of longing, love made visible in conduct, the daily tending of the relationship, steadfastness in sorrow, and prayer. Their opening sentence, "Love Me, that I may love thee," sets the theme. Beside them stand a hundred voices from elsewhere: the Psalms and the Song of Songs, the Gospel and letters of John, Paul, the Qur’an, Plato, Augustine, Rabia, Rumi, Thomas à Kempis, Julian of Norwich, Donne, Herbert, Shakespeare and Tagore, with Spinoza, Machiavelli, Montaigne and Marx to put the questions that a love of God has to meet.
questions: "If thou lovest Me not, My love can in no wise reach thee." How does this stand beside John's "we love him, because he first loved us" and Thompson's picture of a love that pursues?
One passage answers the question of what need good people have of religion. How would you put its answer to Leigh Hunt's Abou Ben Adhem?
The language of longing here uses fire, wine, thirst and the moth at the flame, as the Song of Songs, Rumi and Donne do. What can such language say that plain speech cannot?
"Love the creatures for the sake of God and not for themselves." What would Montaigne say, and how would you reply?
A talk says that if there is no love in prayer one should not pray. How do Isaiah and Julian of Norwich help in thinking about prayer in a dry season?
Many passages say that suffering increases this love. Where do the Psalms and the Gospels leave room for sorrow and protest within it?

outside.why: Jesus states the same reciprocity: the one who loves him will be loved by the Father, and he will show himself to that person.
The Qur’an has the same pairing: if you love God, follow, and God will love you.
The great commandment of Israel puts love of God, with all the heart and soul and might, at the head of religion.
Julian of Norwich was shown that love was the whole meaning of what God had done.
John says we love because God first loved us. This passage adds that unless we love, his love cannot reach us. How do the two statements fit together?
Spinoza thought a true lover of God could not seek to be loved in return. What would be lost from this passage if he were right?
Thompson's poem tells of a love that pursues the one who flees it down the years. Can a love that pursues be kept out by a refusal to love?
Jesus names love of God with the whole heart, soul and mind as the first and great commandment.
Augustine opens his Confessions with the same thought: we are made for God, and the heart is restless until it rests in him.
Paul speaks of the love of God poured into human hearts as a gift of the Spirit.
The psalmist's thirst for God, like a deer's for running water, is the anguish of separation this passage addresses.
Rumi's reed flute laments its cutting from the reed bed, and every listener parted from a beloved understands it.
In Leigh Hunt's poem the man who loves only his fellow men is found at the head of those God loves. How does this passage answer the question the poem raises?
Micah sums up what is required as justice, mercy and a humble walk with God. Which part of his summary would good works alone leave out?
Jesus says that the one who does the Father's will enters the kingdom, not the one who says Lord, Lord. How might the questioner in this passage use that saying, and what is the reply?
Thomas à Kempis begins his book with the same verdict: all is vanity except to love God and serve him.
The first letter of John joins knowing and loving: everyone who loves is born of God and knows God.
Plato's Diotima describes a seeker who, after long ordered striving, suddenly perceives a beauty of another kind.
Pascal holds that it is the heart, not the reason, that experiences God.
Hosea promises knowledge to those who press on to know the Lord, whose coming is as sure as the morning.
Paul sets love above knowledge: the one who loves God is known by him.
On the road to Emmaus the disciples recognized afterwards that their hearts had burned as the word was opened to them.
A psalmist says the same of an undivided heart: there is none on earth that I desire beside thee.
Jesus makes the same exclusive claim on the heart, even above the closest family ties.
The Qur’an contrasts those who love other things as only God should be loved with believers, whose love for God is stronger.
Paul counts everything else as loss beside the knowledge of his Lord.
Rabia of Basra prays to be given neither this world nor the next, since God alone is enough for her.
The Dhammapada advises loving nothing, since the loss of what is loved brings pain. Here one love replaces all the others. Is that the same counsel or its opposite?
The first letter of John defines the love of God as keeping his commandments, and adds that they are not burdensome.
The letter of Jude gives the same charge in six words: keep yourselves in the love of God.
Shakespeare defines human love by its constancy: it does not alter when it finds alteration. What does constancy in human love teach about remaining constant in the love of God?
A psalmist would rather stand at the door of God's house than live at ease elsewhere.
Jesus tells of a merchant who sold all he had for one pearl, a wealth nothing else equals.
The Song of Songs gives the seeker's pain its oldest words: by night I sought him whom my soul loves and found him not.
A psalm from the wilderness speaks of the soul thirsting for God in a dry land, and of a lovingkindness better than life.
The Song of Songs states the union of lovers in one line that later readers took for the soul and God.
FitzGerald's Omar finds paradise in bread, wine, verse and a companion in the wilderness. Does the language of rapture come to religion from human love, or go from religion to it?
Donne asks God to imprison him, since he will never be free otherwise. What do the paradoxes of this station and of his sonnet have in common?
A psalm makes the same appeal to experience: taste and see that the Lord is good.
Jeremiah resolved not to speak of God again, and found the word a fire shut up in his bones.
Augustine addresses the beauty he loved too late, which had been within him while he sought it outside.
Jesus says he came to cast fire upon the earth and longs for it to be kindled.
Jesus tells his followers that they are a light set on a hill, which cannot be hidden.
Dante also finds love to be the mover of the heavens, turning his own desire and will like a wheel.
Aristotle taught that the first cause moves all things as an object of love moves the lover.
Jesus names the measure of love as the laying down of one's life.
This is the verse of the Qur’an from which the passage takes the tree that is neither of the East nor of the West.
The risen Jesus asks Peter three times whether he loves him, and each time answers with a task toward others.
The first letter of John makes love of others the test of love for a God who is not seen.
Paul explains his own restless labour in the same way: love compels him.
Jesus ties love to keeping his word, and promises the presence of God to the one who does both.
This is the sending of the disciples to which the talk looks back.
The Qur’an praises those who feed the poor for love of God and want from them neither reward nor thanks.
Montaigne could explain his love for his friend only by saying: because it was he, because it was I. Is something lost when people are loved for God's sake and not for themselves?
The first letter of John says that perfect love casts out fear.
Machiavelli advised rulers that it is safer to be feared than loved, since love is a bond men break at will. What kind of love does this talk rely on instead?
Paul names love as the greatest of the gifts that remain when prophecy and knowledge have passed away.
Jesus gives the same command in the same form: love one another as I have loved you.
Coleridge's mariner learns that loving all creatures is the best prayer, because God made and loves them all.
Thomas à Kempis praises love as the great good that makes every heavy thing light.
A psalm begins with the plain confession that is the first sign of faith: I love the Lord.
Paul is persuaded that nothing in death or life can separate us from the love of God.
Blake says that love, mercy and pity are where God dwells, and gives love a human form.
Jesus says of a woman who wept at his feet that she loved much.
Marx held that economic conditions are what move history and unite people. This talk says that only the love of God attracts hearts. What does each account explain?
The Qur’an promises that God will appoint love for those who believe and do good.
Tagore sees himself as a small reed flute through which melodies eternally new are breathed, an image for a ray that asks to give light.
A psalmist's love of God's beauty takes the form of one desire: to dwell in his house and behold it.
Isaiah condemns worship offered with the lips while the heart is far away.
Julian hears God say that he is the ground of her beseeching, so that the wish to pray is his gift. What then should a person do who feels no love in prayer?
Jesus commends Mary, who sat and listened, for choosing the one thing needful.
The Qur’an assures the one who calls that God is near and answers.
The Revelation of John reproves a church that has left its first love. If a spark can be fanned into flame, how does a flame cool, and how is it tended?
Paul says that all things work together for good to those who love God.
Hosea pictures God teaching a child to walk and drawing him with bands of love.
Moses came down from the mountain with his face shining, and others could see it.
Paul draws the same contrast between wine and being filled with the Spirit.
The Song of Songs opens with the comparison: thy love is better than wine.
Lovelace, in prison, says that one who is free in his love and in his soul is not confined by walls.
The psalm that Jesus quotes from the cross asks why God has forsaken him. Is there room in the love of God for such a cry?
Habakkuk rejoices in God when every outward comfort has failed, as this prayer does from within prison walls.
The Song of Songs says the same of love's fire: many waters cannot quench it.
When others turned back, Peter answered as the lover does here: to whom shall we go?
The Qur’an says that in the remembrance of God hearts find rest.
Jesus, whom the Gospels present as full of the love of God, wept at a friend's grave. Does that love leave no room for sorrow, or does it change what sorrow is?
The Revelation of John has the same judgement on lukewarmness, neither cold nor hot.
Joseph, whom this passage names, said of his own imprisonment and betrayal that God meant it for good.
The apostles left the council rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to suffer.
Job declares a trust that would hold even if God were to slay him.
The letter to the Hebrews honours those who bore mockery, chains and exile for their faith.
A psalm makes the same plea: for thy sake we are killed all the day long.
Jesus says that the heart follows its treasure, which is why love must rise above what earth and heaven contain.
A psalm of pilgrimage speaks of a soul that longs and even faints for the presence of God.
Herbert is astonished that his shrivelled heart has recovered its greenness, the gladdening this prayer asks for.
Tagore says that the gifts are poured into his small hands through the ages, and still there is room to fill.
Ignatius of Loyola offers his liberty, memory and will, and asks in return only for love and grace.
Kabir hears God say to the one who seeks him everywhere: I am beside thee.
Jesus promises his friends a Comforter who will remain with them always, the companionship this prayer asks for.
Augustine prays in the same way for what he cannot produce in himself: give what you command.
Krishna asks that every act, eating or giving or praying, be done as an offering to him.

psalm-my-soul-thirsteth.text: O God, thou art my God; early will I seek thee: my soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is; To see thy power and thy glory, so as I have seen thee in the sanctuary. Because thy lovingkindness is better than life, my lips shall praise thee

song-my-beloved-is-mine.text: My beloved is mine, and I am his: he feedeth among the lilies

song-sought-him-whom-my-soul-loveth.text: By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not

john-loved-of-my-father.text: He that hath my commandments, and keepeth them, he it is that loveth me: and he that loveth me shall be loved of my Father, and I will love him, and will manifest myself to him

john-lovest-thou-me.text: He saith unto him the third time, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me? Peter was grieved because he said unto him the third time, Lovest thou me? And he said unto him, Lord, thou knowest all things; thou knowest that I love thee. Jesus saith unto him, Feed my sheep

philippians-count-all-things-but-loss.text: Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ

john-epistle-keep-his-commandments.text: For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments: and his commandments are not grievous

psalm-taste-and-see.text: O taste and see that the Lord is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him

luke-did-not-our-heart-burn.text: And they said one to another, Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures

luke-fire-on-the-earth.text: I am come to send fire on the earth; and what will I, if it be already kindled

romans-love-shed-abroad.text: And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us

psalm-for-thy-sake-are-we-killed.text: Yea, for thy sake are we killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter

matthew-loveth-father-or-mother-more.text: He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me

jude-keep-yourselves-in-the-love.text: Keep yourselves in the love of God, looking for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life

psalm-i-love-the-lord.text: I love the Lord, because he hath heard my voice and my supplications. Because he hath inclined his ear unto me, therefore will I call upon him as long as I live

isaiah-draw-near-with-their-mouth.text: Wherefore the Lord said, Forasmuch as this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me, and their fear toward me is taught by the precept of men

luke-mary-hath-chosen.text: And Jesus answered and said unto her, Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her

corinthians-love-of-christ-constraineth.text: For the love of Christ constraineth us; because we thus judge, that if one died for all, then were all dead: And that he died for all, that they which live should not henceforth live unto themselves, but unto him which died for them, and rose again

quran-stauncher-in-love.text: Yet of mankind are some who take unto themselves (objects of worship which they set as) rivals to Allah, loving them with a love like (that which is the due) of Allah (only) - those who believe are stauncher in their love for Allah - Oh, that those who do evil had but known, (on the day) when they behold the doom, that power belongeth wholly to Allah, and that Allah is severe in punishment!

quran-if-ye-love-allah-follow-me.text: Say, (O Muhammad, to mankind): If ye love Allah, follow me; Allah will love you and forgive you your sins. Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.

shakespeare-love-is-not-love.text: Love is not love / Which alters when it alteration finds, / Or bends with the remover to remove: / O no! it is an ever-fixed mark / That looks on tempests and is never shaken
shakespeare-love-is-not-love.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

plato-nature-of-wondrous-beauty.text: He who has been instructed thus far in the things of love, and who has learned to see the beautiful in due order and succession, when he comes toward the end will suddenly perceive a nature of wondrous beauty
plato-nature-of-wondrous-beauty.author: Plato
